source.title: Efficient Decoder Scaling Strategy for Neural Routing Solvers
source.authors: Qingze Luo; Fu Luo; Ke Li; Zhen-Kun Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. The extracted text contains corrupted encoding characters in places, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It empirically tests scaling relationships in neural routing solvers using optimality gap rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy loss. Its findings are analogous to scaling-law claims but do not test the specified language-model versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures optimality gap for neural routing solvers, not held-out pretraining loss for language models. Therefore, no result maps directly to V1–V7. The paper cites Kaplan et al. and uses power-law fits, but cited results are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: Power-law scaling fits on a new system, Transformer TSP solvers trained by supervised next-node prediction. This bears on V5 (form beyond text pretraining), but uses optimality gap, not held-out loss, over ~1.3M–144M params.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that parameter count alone does not predict optimality gap, and that depth scaling beats width scaling in parameter, data and inference-compute efficiency. They propose deep-narrow design principles and validate them in-domain and on larger TSP instances.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits empirical power laws to routing-solver optimality gap against parameter count, training data size, and inference compute; the target systems, outcomes, and compute setting differ from the original language-model held-out-loss studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling fits and efficiency differ between depth and width scaling; the global parameter-count fit is substantially less accurate than fits that separate depth and width.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed ~1.3M parameters, reshaping D=6,W=128 to D=96,W=32 cuts TSP100 gap from 0.464% to 0.184% (Table 2). Depth exponents are ~1.0 versus 0.24–0.40 for width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TSP Transformer solvers, model shape at fixed parameter count strongly changes performance (contrary to the LM V4 analogue).

fits_no_version.finding: Gap falls as a power law in inference beam-search FLOPs, with exponents 0.82–1.71 depending on architecture; a shifted power law fits gap versus inference time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time compute scaling in routing solvers follows power laws whose exponent depends on depth versus width.

record.problems: The experiments focus on TSP and a parameter range from 1M to 144M; the paper identifies investigation at larger scales and other routing problems as future work. Reported results use optimality gap rather than language-model held-out loss.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcomes were left out. Rows record the paper's aggregate fit results relevant as analogous scaling findings; the many per-model solution-gap tables and unrelated ablations are not separate results on the claim's language-model loss measures.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation for training compute.
Depth/width at fixed N studied only for TSP solvers, not LMs (see fits_no_version).
Held-out loss not measured (optimality gap only). Scale range is about two orders of magnitude. TSP100 only.
No comparison of fitting choices for LM exponents.

missing.what: Fixed-parameter shape comparison: D=6,W=128 vs D=24,W=64 vs D=96,W=32 at ~1.3M params, gap 0.464/0.297/0.184% on TSP100.
Limited-data multi-epoch (0.1M samples, 60 epochs) comparison of deep vs wide models.
Shifted power-law fits of gap vs inference time (R2 0.909–0.998).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's guess that the study tests nothing is too strict, since V5 explicitly covers other domains. The links rest on optimality gap standing in for loss, which is a weaker match. Inference-compute rows are excluded from V5. The study cites Kaplan only to borrow the functional form.

versions.untested_parts: Tests routing-solver optimality gap, not held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Does not test whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Does not test loss-minimising language-model parameter and token allocations at a fixed training-compute budget.
Tests depth and width effects on routing-solver optimality gap, not language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Does not test language-model scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Reports routing-solver solution quality, not language-model downstream task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Reports setup- and architecture-dependent fits for routing-solver optimality gap, not fitted language-model loss exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits.

rows.subject: 12 decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a single power law to optimality gap versus parameter count across all 12 models.
rows.measure: Optimality gap versus parameter count; coefficient of determination and mean prediction error
rows.value: R2 ≈ 0.79 (Figure 2(a)); R2 = 0.794 and average prediction error = 34.39% (text and figure description)
rows.note: The paper says this fit is relatively loose and parameter count alone is insufficient for accurate prediction in this routing-solver setting. This is not a result about language-model loss.
rows.check: Single power law in N gives a loose fit (R2 0.794, 34.39% error); the power-law form holds only roughly once shape varies.

rows.subject: Decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a bivariate power law in model width and depth, then express the fit using parameter count and depth-to-width ratio.

conditions.value: bivariate fit using evaluation results of 12 models

rows.measure: Fitted exponents for parameter count and depth-to-width ratio
rows.value: Doubling parameter count at fixed A reduces the gap to 71% (2−0.5) of its original value; doubling A at fixed parameter count reduces it to 76% (2−0.4)
rows.note: This is a routing-solver optimality-gap fit, not a language-model loss law.
rows.check: The power-law form holds only with an added shape term: doubling D/W at fixed N cuts the gap to 76%, comparable to doubling N (71%). Unlike the LM form, where shape matters little.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, Equations 5–6 and accompanying paragraph: doubling N at fixed A gives 71%; doubling A at fixed N gives 76%.
